kurz: Why a discount to value protects against your own mistakes, how Buffett moved from Graham's cigar butts to highly profitable companies, and what fourteen weak years reveal about the limits of the oldest school of equity analysis.

bloecke.md:
Value investing distinguishes between price and value. The price is the market price of the share; the value results from what the company earns. Today this sounds obvious, but in 1934 it ran counter to common practice. In that year, five years after the crash of 1929, Benjamin Graham and David Dodd published *Security Analysis*. At the time, equity analysis consisted mainly of rumours, price lists and insider knowledge. Graham and Dodd approached it as a craft. They read the balance sheet, estimated earning power, derived a value from it and only then looked at the price.

The method rests on two principles. First, a share is a stake in a business and not merely a ticker symbol whose price you bet on. Second, the market supplies prices, but no judgements about value. Investors who take the second principle seriously do not need a price target from outside, but they do need their own estimate and the patience to wait for a price well below it.

## Mr Market

Graham illustrated this idea with a parable. A business partner called [[Mr Market]] names a price every day at which he would buy the investor's share or sell his own. He is manic-depressive. On good days he sees only opportunities and names absurdly high prices; on bad days he sees only dangers and offers his share at knock-down prices. His offer creates no obligation. You can accept it, but you never have to. Buffett concluded from this, in essence, that Mr Market's pocketbook is useful, but his judgement is not.

The parable describes the way the whole school works and is more than a psychological add-on. Price fluctuations are thus less a risk than an offer you can take advantage of. However, this only applies to investors who have their own estimate of value and do not invest on credit. Without your own estimate, a falling price is just bad news. Anyone who works with borrowed money can be forced to sell when prices fall instead of taking advantage of Mr Market's offers.

The [[Margin of safety (Sicherheitsmarge)|margin of safety]] is the gap between estimated value and the price paid. It serves as a buffer for your own mistakes and not as a reward for a good idea. Such mistakes include a wrong assumption, an overlooked liability or a business that develops worse than assumed. The question is therefore less whether the value is 100 than whether it is still above the price even in an unfavourable scenario.

Graham derived testable rules from this. The P/E ratio should be no more than 15, measured on average earnings over three years, and the price-to-book ratio no more than 1.5. Graham allowed a higher price-to-book ratio with a correspondingly lower P/E, as long as the product of the two was no more than 22.5. Current assets should be at least twice as high as current liabilities. The rules also required twenty years of uninterrupted dividends and ten years without a loss-making year. His strictest test was the net-net criterion. Under it, he only bought when the market value was below two thirds of current assets minus all liabilities. He valued fixed assets and earning power at zero.

The calculations belong to valuation theory; what matters here is the attitude behind the rules. Value should come from the balance sheet and not from a forecast. Graham distrusted every estimate of the future, so he bought assets, diversified broadly and deliberately formed no opinion about individual companies. Buffett later called such shares [[Cigar butt|cigar butts]], because they have only one last free puff left in them. The approach is limited from the outset. It works with small sums in market niches that nobody searches, requires constant buying and selling, and cannot be scaled up at will.

## The purchase of See's Candies in 1972

Buffett regards the purchase of See's Candies as the turning point. The price paid was $25 million for a company with $30 million in revenue, just under $5 million in pre-tax profit and $8 million of capital employed. The price was therefore around three times the capital tied up in the business. With around $2 million in after-tax profit, this gave a P/E of around 12.5 and a product of P/E and price-to-book ratio of around 39. Under Graham's rules, this purchase should never have taken place. The investment became the most instructive of his career.

The last row of the table is the most revealing. The additional $77 million of pre-tax profit came from $32 million of additional capital, which is around 240% on the newly invested money. A business that can grow without much additional capital becomes more valuable with every year. For the buyer, a long holding period is then an advantage. With a cigar butt it is a disadvantage, because the business eats up its assets while the buyer waits for a higher valuation. Buffett's statement in his 1989 shareholder letter that it is far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price follows from this calculation and is not a matter of taste. Buffett added that Munger had understood this early on. What exactly makes up quality and what it costs to pay too much for it is covered in the next lesson.

bloecke.md:
## Ratios in value analysis

Every value ratio relates the price to a measure of earnings or assets. None of these ratios is a valuation in itself. They serve as sorting aids that raise questions but do not answer them. Numerator and denominator must match. The share price belongs with equity measures, enterprise value with measures of total capital.

Whether a share is cheap only ever becomes clear in comparison, for example with its own history, the sector or the level of interest rates. On 18 September 2026, the Shiller P/E of the US market stood at 40.9, against a historical average of 17.4. The trailing P/E of the S&P 500 was 26.1 on the same day, compared with a long-term average of 16.2. For the overall US market excluding financials, Damodaran reports an EV/EBIT of 25.7 as of January 2026.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula gives the fair price-to-book ratio of a steadily growing company. By this formula, a low P/B first of all says something about returns and is not automatically a discount. If the return on equity is below the cost of equity, the company belongs below book value. The low valuation is then appropriate.
bloecke.beispiel: With r = 9.7% (average for the mainly German companies in the KPMG cost of capital study 2025) and g = 1%, an ROE of 6% gives a P/B of 0.57. A price of 0.6 times book value would therefore be fair and not cheap. An ROE of 15% gives 1.61.

bloecke.md:
A [[Value trap|value trap]] is a share that looks cheap and stays cheap because earnings fall faster than the price. Typical signs are:

- With cyclical stocks, the P/E is misleading. It is lowest when profits are highest and therefore most at risk.
- Operating cash flow lags persistently behind reported profit, and receivables and inventories grow faster than revenue.
- The company destroys capital by reinvesting in a shrinking business instead of paying money back or buying back shares.
- High debt creates time pressure, because the thesis then lacks the years it would need.

Every value thesis therefore needs a reason why the discount should disappear. Possible triggers are a change in capital allocation, a change of management, the sale of the problem business, buybacks below value or a takeover. Without such a trigger, the share can stay cheap permanently. The Piotroski F-score for balance sheet quality within the value universe and the Altman Z-score for insolvency risk serve as rule-based pre-filters.

## The value factor's weak phase

Since Fama/French (1993), value has also been treated as a measurable factor. The [[HML]] (High Minus Low) factor buys the shares with a high ratio of book value to market value and sells those with a low ratio. Over a hundred years, from July 1926 to July 2026, this long-short construct returned a geometric average of 3.59% a year. The result is statistically well established. On the way there, however, there were deep and long periods of losses.

HML reached its peak in December 2006. By September 2020, the factor had lost 57.8%. This was the deepest value slump since 1926. Over the full fourteen years from 2007 to 2020, it came to minus 5.67% a year, or minus 55.8% cumulatively. Since January 2021, it has been recovering at 8.71% a year, a cumulative plus 59.4%, which, however, does not yet make up for the loss. In July 2026, HML is still around 30% below its old high, which has therefore not been regained for 19.6 years.

bloecke.md:
There are several competing explanations for the weak phase, none of which has been conclusively proven. Falling interest rates favoured cash flows lying far in the future and thus growth companies. The platform economy with its economies of scale has widened the lead of the most successful companies. In addition, there is a measurement problem. Book value only partly captures research, brands and software, so a company that invests mainly in these areas appears expensive by this ratio. Moreover, return patterns lose their effect once they are published. For 97 return patterns examined, McLean/Pontiff find on average 26% lower returns outside the original sample period and 58% lower returns after publication.

Minus 5.67% a year does not mean that value shares fell, because the market rose strongly in those years. Value shares lagged behind growth shares. Nor is a long weak phase proof against the factor. For HML, 14.3% of all rolling ten-year windows since 1926 were negative, as were 7.4% of all twenty-year windows. Conversely, two strong years such as 2021 and 2022 do not prove a comeback either.

HML's 3.59% comes from a long-short portfolio without costs, taxes, spreads or short-selling constraints. A long-only value ETF has only a fraction of this factor exposure, because its return depends mainly on the overall market (market beta). It also pays a management fee, trading costs and turnover costs. On top of this comes a selection problem. For smart beta indices, Huang/Song/Xiang show an excess return of around 3% a year in the backtest before the product was launched, and minus 0.5% to minus 1% afterwards. For 204 anomalies, Chen/Velikov arrive at an average of around 0.5% a year after costs. Realistically, the difference between factor strategies and the broad market after costs lies between about minus 1 and plus 0.5 percentage points a year. Along the way, you have to accept double-digit shortfalls and weak phases of ten to twenty years.

## Implementation in Germany

Three points count when it comes to implementation. The first is costs. In the ten-year period from 2012 to 2021, equity UCITS in the EU cost 1.50% a year under active management, 0.53% as passive funds other than ETFs and 0.31% as ETFs. Net returns were 9.4% compared with 10.6% and 10.4% a year. The second point is success rates. In the ten years to June 2025, 16.3% of active US large-cap value funds did better than their passive counterpart; for US large-cap growth funds, the figure was 2.8%. Among large US stocks, active selection in the value segment therefore has measurably better prospects than in the other segments, but only a minority succeeds.

Third, tax weighs more heavily on value than on other investment styles, because the method forces you to sell as soon as the discount has disappeared. Price gains on directly held shares are subject to 26.375% tax, made up of 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, excluding church tax. Anyone who switches their entire holdings every year pays this tax every year. If the shares are held, it would only be due at the end, and the tax amount would remain invested until then.

bloecke.md: The calculation leaves out product costs, dividends, the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) and the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale). It therefore only shows the effect of tax and says nothing about products. With an accumulating fund, the advance lump sum brings part of the tax forward. With a base interest rate (Basiszins) of 3.20% for 2026, this effect is no longer negligible. Regardless of this, a style with annual switching costs around one seventh of final wealth in Germany, even before the quality of the selection plays a role. Investors who choose value as their style should factor this disadvantage into the excess return they expect.

Value investing is more than buying low ratios. It rests on the claim that the market assumes a worse future for a business than the business deserves. This claim needs a justification, a trigger and a time frame you can endure, if necessary a full decade.

mitnehmen: Price and value are different quantities, and the margin of safety between them serves as a buffer for your own errors and not as profit.
Mr Market's offers create no obligation and can only be used with your own estimate of value and without credit.
The shift from Graham to Munger has a mathematical basis: with a high return on additional capital, the value of a business rises over time, whereas with a cigar butt it falls.
A low P/B says something about return on equity first, and if this is below the cost of equity, the low valuation is appropriate.
The value factor returned 3.59% a year over a hundred years but lost almost 58% between 2006 and 2020, so investors in this style must expect deviations that can last a decade.

High Minus Low, the academic value factor according to Fama/French. It buys shares with a high ratio of book value to market value and sells those with a low ratio. HML is a long-short construct without costs and not an investable product.
Share that looks cheap and stays cheap because earning power declines faster than the price. Its hallmark is the absence of a trigger that would end the discount.
Buffett's image for Graham's asset-based purchases. It refers to a discarded company that is still good for one last free puff. The approach cannot be scaled up at will and requires constant selling.
